transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-03-28
Start: 14:00 UTC
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Olivia Chen (Redwood AE), Marcus Patel (Redwood SE), Sara Vance (Lakeshore Head of ML Ops), Derek Liu (Lakeshore Infra), Priya Sharma (CTO)

[00:00] Olivia: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick agenda today — run through the benchmark numbers Marcus ran this week, talk TTFT and streaming, then agree next steps.
[00:18] Sara: Yep, thanks Olivia. We had a few painful spikes last week in prod, so TTFT is our top priority.
[00:25] Marcus: Great, I pushed a couple runs to the bench sheet, two main variants: hosted (multi-tenant) defaults, and dedicated with quantized kernels. I also tried streaming chunk sizes 1 and 4.
[00:40] Derek: Quick context — our 99th tail at baseline is around 1.4s for 1024 seq, which is too high for UI, so trying to get that under 600ms.
[00:52] Marcus: Right, so headline: hosted default TTFT median ~220ms, 95th ~380ms, 99th ~680ms for 512 seq. For 1024 seq median jumps to ~320ms, 99th ~1.1s.
[01:12] Marcus: On dedicated GPUs with fused/flash kernels and int8 quant, median TTFT for 512 is ~95-110ms, 95th ~160ms, 99th ~240ms. For 1024 median ~150ms, 99th ~420ms.
[01:30] Priya: Those dedicated numbers look promising. Is that with streaming enabled?
[01:34] Marcus: The dedicated numbers I just quoted were non-streaming generation. With streaming turned on and small chunk size, TTFT for the first partial token actually goes down ~10-20ms in some runs — because we start flush earlier — but we do see a small increase in overall tail due to more context switching across micro-batches.
[01:55] Sara: Wait, can you clarify that? I thought streaming always improves first-byte latency.
[02:00] Marcus: It usually does for perceived latency — you see a token sooner — but the runtime overhead for streaming (flushes, more RPCs) can hurt throughput and tail for high-concurrency patterns. So you trade a better time-to-first-byte for potentially worse 99th under heavy load.
[02:18] Derek: That matches what we saw last Friday — streaming reduced our initial render, but under concurrency the backend went to 95th spikes.
[02:26] Olivia: Important to note Redwood can route by policy — you can enable streaming for interactive UIs and fallback to non-streaming for bulk jobs.
[02:35] Marcus: On kernel choices: I tested standard cu kernels, Triton fused attention, and flash-attn variants. Flash/fused gave best latency at 512/1024, especially for 16k head dims we use, but for 2048 sequences the memory patterns change and sometimes Triton wins. So kernel selection should be sequence-length aware.
[02:58] Priya: So we need an auto-selector in our runtime?
[03:01] Marcus: Exactly — Redwood's runtime already has a kernel selector but we recommended a pass based on your observed sequence length distribution. I want to run a dedicated kernel-selection pass against Lakeshore's real trace to pick defaults.
[03:12] Sara: We also care about the TTFT cold-start — e.g., when KV cache is empty vs warm. Any numbers there?
[03:18] Marcus: Cold-start (no KV cache) adds about 40-70ms per request on most models in the benchmarks. Warm KV cache reduces steady state token cost but doesn't fully eliminate first-token overhead unless you're prefix-caching.
[03:30] Derek: On KV cache, our infra team is a bit worried about memory growth if we keep many prefixes cached in Dedicated. Any guidance?
[03:36] Marcus: You can bound cache by policy (LRU, per-customer cap). For the POC we recommend prefix caching for sessioned UIs and LRU for ad-hoc. We'll include sample configs.
[03:46] Sara: Back to numbers — can you share the bench sheet link now?
[03:50] Marcus: I'll drop it in the notes after. The key rows: 512 / hosted / median 220ms, 512 / dedicated / median 95ms, 1024 / hosted / median 320ms, 2048 / hosted / median 760ms. With int8 quant we saw ~15-25% CPU/GPU time reduction and corresponding latency improvements.
[04:10] Priya: Do we lose quality with int8? We care about hallucination rates on our financial prompts.
[04:15] Marcus: In our eval sets quality delta was small for NLL/QA style tasks; for sensitive regulatory text we recommend running a small eval harness. Redwood can help run the eval on your in-house prompts.
[04:25] Olivia: On security concerns — Derek raised earlier about SSO and audit logs, we're ready to share SOC2/ISO docs and detail log retention.
[04:32] Derek: Yes please, and KMS integration specifics. Our security team needs to know about HSM or KMIP options.
[04:38] Olivia: We'll send the security pack along with pricing.
[04:41] Marcus: A couple of practical knobs we discussed: batch size, micro-batch flush interval, and chunk size for streaming. For Lakeshore's throughput (~400 reqs/min peak) I recommend micro-batch size 8 with max latency target 150ms for frontend flows.
[04:57] Sara: How does that interact with autoscaling? If we set small micro-batches, do we need more nodes?
[05:02] Marcus: Yes small batches reduce per-request latency but increase GPU utilization; autoscaling config can add nodes earlier. With dedicated reserved capacity you can set burst pools to handle spikes without hurting baseline cost.
[05:14] Derek: Cost question — what's the delta between hosted and a dedicated pool that hits your 99th targets?
[05:19] Olivia: I'll send a tailored cost sheet but rough ballpark: dedicated committed monthly is higher fixed cost but reduces per-token unit cost by 30-50% at scale and gives predictable latency SLOs. We'll include example amortizations.
[05:33] Marcus: Quick demo note: I can enable kernel selector beta on a test pool and run your trace overnight; that'll produce a recommended profile for 512/1024/2048.
[05:43] Priya: That would be useful. Also want to try streaming canary for our support UI only.
[05:48] Marcus: We can run streaming canary at 10% traffic, monitor for 99th tail increase, and auto rollback if it breaches thresholds.
[05:55] Derek: What metrics should we watch in the canary?
[05:58] Marcus: TTFT median, TTFT 95/99, token throughput, GPU util, and error rates. We also add a synthetic trace that simulates worst-case sequence lengths.
[06:08] Olivia: Any competitor considerations? Sara?
[06:11] Sara: We looked at Anthropic and AWS Bedrock; Bedrock had some nice integration but our main concern was lack of predictable dedicated pools and variable kernel optimizations.
[06:21] Marcus: Ok, action items summary — I'll run the kernel-selection and post results by Friday. Olivia will share pricing + security docs. Derek to share prod traces.
[06:30] Priya: One more question — model pinning and rollbacks if a kernel update regresses.
[06:34] Marcus: Redwood supports model variant pinning and rollout policies. We can do canary then auto-roll back to previous kernel/model configuration if quality or latency regresses.
[06:44] Derek: Good. On the KV cache LRU policy example, can you provide a config snippet?
[06:49] Marcus: Yes I'll include a snippet in the bench notes.
[06:52] Olivia: Great. Any final Qs?
[06:55] Sara: No, just please include the bench link and the security pack.
[06:58] Olivia: Will do. Thanks everyone, talk Friday for updates.

[End of transcript]

Notes: transcription contains a few mis-hearings ("KV cash" in a couple automated lines), speaker attributions may be slightly off in spots. Bench sheet link: https://redwood-internal.example/bench/lakeshore-2028-03-28 (shared after call). Security pack link: https://redwood-internal.example/security-pack.zip (sent via email).
